profiles.name: Arthur Evans
profiles.description: Arthur Evans was a Denver, Colorado Quaker physician and lifelong pacifist who refused all or part of his federal income taxes every year from the early 1940s onward, donating the refused amounts (and sometimes double) to charitable causes. In 1963 he was sentenced to 90 days in Jefferson County Jail in Colorado for contempt of court after refusing to provide financial records to the Internal Revenue Service. He served the full 90-day term. He was one of only six people confirmed imprisoned for war tax resistance in the United States between 1945 and 1965. In a 1962 AP interview he stated: "I won't pay the tax for war voluntarily. This way the responsibility for committing the immoral act is on the government."

profiles.name: Wilbert Lee
profiles.description: Wilbert Lee was one of two Black men, with Freddie Lee Pitts, falsely convicted of the August 1963 kidnapping, robbery and murder of two white gas-station attendants in Port St. Joe, Florida. They were convicted with no material evidence, on confessions obtained through beatings and threats, and sentenced to death in 1968; in 1968 a key witness admitted she had lied under police threat. Lee, a pulpwood cutter at whose home Pitts had attended a party that night, confessed after being told his wife would be harmed. After the Florida Supreme Court ordered a new grand jury in 1969 (Black citizens had been excluded), an all-white jury again convicted them in 1972 and they were sentenced to be electrocuted — even though another man, Curtis Adams Jr., had confessed to the killings. They were finally pardoned by Governor Reubin Askew in 1975. Documented in The Black Panther (April 27, 1974).

profiles.name: Frank Lott
profiles.description:
Frank Lott was incarcerated at Attica in 1971 and helped establish the Attica Liberation Faction. The prisoners' manifesto named him as one of five representatives authorized to negotiate with state and prison officials. The group organized political education and demands for improved prison conditions.

This profile concerns political organizing during imprisonment. It does not establish that the original conviction was politically motivated. Exact custody boundaries and the later release history remain unresolved.

A 1971 federal decision records a fifty-years-to-life sentence imposed on June 5, 1962, after a guilty plea to second-degree murder. In later litigation Lott alleged that parole decisions penalized his legal work and involvement in the Attica manifesto. The 1979 court dismissed his habeas petition for failure to exhaust state remedies and allowed him an opportunity to replead a First Amendment retaliation claim; it did not find that retaliation had been proved.
profiles.finding: Freedom Archives We Are Attica PDF includes captioned Frank Lott closeup; scan extraction and rights review pending.
